The Uncompromising Necessity of Absolute Free Speech: A Defense of Expression Without Exception

Introduction

Freedom of expression stands as the cornerstone of democratic civilization, the foundational liberty upon which all other rights rest. Yet in an era of heightened sensitivity, viral misinformation, and provocative rhetoric, there exists growing momentum to carve out exceptions—to place guardrails around speech deemed hateful, false, or offensive. This impulse, however well-intentioned, represents one of the most dangerous philosophical errors a free society can commit. The only intellectually coherent, morally defensible, and practically sustainable framework for protecting liberty is an absolute interpretation of free speech: one that legally protects all forms of expression without exception. Anything less transforms the most fundamental right of self-governance into a conditional privilege dispensed at the discretion of those in power.

This essay argues that absolute free speech protection is not merely preferable but essential, because exceptions inevitably expand, because the power to silence is the power to control, because counterspeech rather than censorship is the only remedy consistent with human dignity, and because the abstract harms attributed to unregulated expression are dwarfed by the concrete, documented catastrophes produced by speech restriction throughout history.

I. The Indivisibility of the First Principle

The central logical objection to a conditional free speech framework is deceptively simple: rights that are permitted to be violated in their extreme applications are not rights at all—they are permissions, revocable whenever a majority or a government concludes that their exercise has crossed some subjective threshold. A right that exists only so long as its expression pleases or at least does not deeply disturb the powerful is a right defined out of existence.

Consider the architecture of rights more broadly. We do not say that freedom of religion applies only to religious doctrines the state finds morally acceptable. We do not hold that the right against unreasonable searches applies merely when police officers have benign intentions. We recognize that rights necessarily protect conduct—and expression—that we may find objectionable, because the purpose of enshrining a right is precisely to shield the individual from collective disapproval. Speech is no different. To declare that expression shall be protected except when it is hateful, false, or offensive is to void the protection entirely, for each of these categories is inherently subjective and endlessly expandable.

Justice Hugo Black understood this with uncommon clarity. His absolutist reading of the First Amendment—"no law means no law"—was not naïveté but profound structural realism. He recognized that the moment a state acquires the power to distinguish between protected and unprotected speech, it possesses the very mechanism of tyrannical control that the Bill of Rights was designed to prevent. The First Amendment does not say "Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech, except where speech is harmful, offensive, or untrue." It says no law. That plain language is not an accident or an oversight; it is a firewall, and every exception punched through that firewall weakens the entire structure of liberty.

II. The Historical Record: Speech Restrictions Serve Power

If intellectual arguments for absolute free speech seem abstract, the historical record renders them devastatingly concrete. Across centuries and civilizations, every regime that has curtailed speech has done so not in defense of the persecuted but in service of the powerful.

The British colonial government prosecuted colonists for seditious libel—not because the criticisms of the crown were false, but because they were true and therefore threatening. The Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 were used almost exclusively by the Federalist Party to jail Republican newspaper editors, demonstrating with painful immediacy that speech laws are weaponized along partisan lines. Lincoln suspended habeas corpus and jailed newspaper editors during the Civil War. Woodrow Wilson's Espionage and Sedition Acts of 1917–1918 sent Eugene V. Debs—a presidential candidate—to prison for questioning the morality of the draft. The McCarthy-era persecution of American communists and sympathizers did not protect society; it destroyed careers, entrenched fear, and chilled political discourse for a generation.

International examples compound the indictment. The Rwandan government weaponized hate speech laws before and during the 1994 genocide, using the power to define what constituted "divisionist" speech as a mechanism of ethnic mobilization. Turkey routinely prosecutes citizens under Article 301 for "insulting Turkishness," overwhelmingly targeting Kurdish and Armenian voices. Russia's anti-extremism legislation has been deployed against political dissidents, journalists, and ordinary citizens who share articles on social media. In China, the criminalization of "picking quarrels and provoking trouble"—a speech crime—has been used to silence human rights lawyers and whistleblowers.

In every case, the pattern is identical: the state first claims the power to restrict speech for a narrow, acknowledged good—public order, national security, protection of the vulnerable—and then progressively expands that power until it serves the interests of those who wield it. This is not a bug in the system. It is the system. Speech regulation does not merely permit authoritarianism; it is the instrument through which authoritarianism operates, because the ability to control what can be said is the ability to control what can be thought, organized, and acted upon.

Justice Blackstone's principle—that prior restraint is the essence of censorship—remains true across all forms of suppression. Whether the state prevents speech before it occurs or punishes it afterward, the effect is identical: the citizen must first secure permission from authority before speaking freely. This inversion of the relationship between the individual and the state transforms free subjects into supplicants.

III. The Failure of Taxonomies: Why "Hate Speech," "Misinformation," and "Offense" Cannot Be Legally Defined

Proponents of speech restrictions argue that some categories of expression are so inherently harmful that they fall outside the protective scope of free expression. Three categories dominate contemporary discourse: hate speech, misinformation, and offensive content. Each, upon rigorous examination, proves to be a category that cannot be coherently or justly delineated by law.

Hate Speech

The concept of hate speech presupposes that expressions of contempt, animosity, or hostility based on group identity can be identified, categorized, and suppressed in a manner consistent with justice. In practice, this is an impossibility. Who defines what constitutes hate? The phrase "hate speech" is powerful precisely because it conflates two entirely different phenomena: genuine incitements to violence (already prohibited under the Brandenburg standard of imminent lawless action), and speech that expresses deeply offensive views about racial, religious, ethnic, or other groups.

The conflation is deliberate and dangerous. When a college student asserts that certain racial groups are intellectually inferior, the statement is repugnant. When a cartoonist depicts the Prophet Muhammad, the image is profoundly offensive to millions. When a protester carries a sign claiming that homosexuality is sinful, the sentiment causes deep pain. None of these expressions, however, constitutes a direct incitement to violence. They are, rather, assertions of viewpoint—however odious—and their suppression requires the state to make a determination about which viewpoints are too abhorrent to be tolerated. That determination is inherently political, inherently subjective, and inherently subject to manipulation.

The European model, widely cited by proponents of hate speech laws, provides no comfort. Germany's Volksverhetzung (incitement to hatred) laws have been used to prosecute not only neo-Nazis but also ordinary citizens who question aspects of Holocaust historiography—effectively making historical inquiry a criminal offense under the theory that certain truths are too dangerous to deny. Hungary's criminal Code has been used against opposition figures who criticize government policy. The European Court of Human Rights has upheld the conviction of Austrian politician Susanne Winter for calling the Prophet Muhammad a pedophile—a statement that, while shocking, expressed a viewpoint rooted in specific textual claims that are matters of theological debate. The power to criminalize opinions one finds hateful inevitably becomes the power to criminalize dissent.

Misinformation

The case against the regulation of false speech appears, on its surface, more compelling. Surely, one might argue, a society may prohibit the deliberate dissemination of provably false information that threatens public health or safety? The COVID-19 pandemic brought this argument to the forefront, as governments worldwide censored claims about the virus's origins, transmission, and treatment that were subsequently—in some cases—shown to have contained elements of truth.

The fundamental problem with regulating misinformation is epistemological: the state must first determine what is true, and then punish those who dissent from that determination. But truth is not a settled commodity delivered whole from authority; it is a process of contestation, falsification, and revision. Galileo was persecuted for asserting what we now know to be true. The establishment of germ theory was resisted by medical authorities. The link between smoking and cancer was disputed for decades by scientists funded by the tobacco industry. During the early AIDS crisis, those who proposed that HIV caused AIDS faced institutional skepticism. In every era, what the establishment labeled "misinformation" included claims that were later vindicated.

Moreover, misinformation laws are invariably asymmetric. During the run-up to the Iraq War, the United States government disseminated extensive false claims about weapons of mass destruction. No official was prosecuted for this misinformation, which was far more consequential in human terms than anything an individual citizen might post online. The pattern is always the same: those in power define misinformation as any claim that threatens their interests or narrative, while their own falsehoods enjoy de facto immunity. Speech regulation thus does not eliminate falsehood; it concentrates the authority to define truth in the hands of the already powerful.

The marketplace of ideas metaphor, often invoked dismissively, captures a genuine truth: no institution, no matter how well-resourced or well-intentioned, has demonstrated the capacity to arbitrate truth reliably enough to justify granting it the power of law. The alternative to a marketplace of information is not a purified information environment but a controlled one—and controlled information environments are the hallmark of authoritarian states throughout history.

Offensive Content

The claim that speech should be restricted because it causes offense is the weakest of the three arguments and, paradoxically, the most widely practiced in Western societies through hate speech codes, workplace speech regulations, and campus speech restrictions. If offense were a constitutionally sufficient basis for suppressing expression, no speech would be safe, for virtually every idea that has ever advanced human progress was at one time deeply offensive to some portion of the population.

The abolition of slavery was offensive to slaveholders. The enfranchisement of women offended those who believed in the natural subordination of women. The civil rights movement was offensive to segregationists. The legalization of same-sex marriage offended millions who held sincere religious convictions. The publication of portraits of Christ embedded in urine offended devout Christians. The publication of cartoons depicting the Prophet Muhammad offended devout Muslims. In each case, the choice is the same: protect expression that offends, or empower the offended to silence their opponents.

There is no limiting principle. If the state may suppress speech because it causes offense, then any group that can demonstrate sufficient offense can suppress any expression it dislikes. The history of blasphemy laws from colonial India to contemporary Pakistan, from the prosecution of Salman Rushdie to the murder of Charlie Hebdo editors, illustrates not that blasphemy regulation is too permissive but that it is conceptually incoherent. The faithful will always find offense, and the powerful will always accept the argument that their particular offense warrants legal remedy. Offense is not a standard; it is an emotion, and no free society can permit emotions to function as criminal statutes without dismantling the foundation of liberty itself.

IV. The Power to Silence Shapes Political Reality Directly

The argument for absolute free speech is not merely philosophical; it is rooted in the concrete mechanics of political power. Governments that can restrict speech can shape public perception, and the ability to shape public perception is the ability to determine political outcomes. This is not speculative; it is observable in real time.

In Singapore, defamation laws have been used systematically by the People's Action Party leadership to bankrupt opposition politicians and silence critical media. In Venezuela, the Resorte Law and subsequent regulations shut down or co-opted broadcasters to ensure that the Chávez and Maduro governments controlled their public narratives. In Egypt, the regime of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has imprisoned thousands under anti-terrorism and anti-fake-news laws, effectively eliminating the political opposition's capacity to communicate. In India, sedition laws enacted by the British colonial government remain on the books and are routinely deployed against journalists, activists, and academics who criticize the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

In each case, the speech restrictions were initially justified by reference to recognized goods—national security, public order, prevention of disinformation. In each case, the result was the consolidation of political power in the hands of those who controlled the instruments of censorship. The causal chain is direct: suppress speech, control the public narrative, control the political process, entrench power. Speech regulation does not protect the public from manipulation; it delivers the tools of manipulation to the state.

Free speech, by contrast, is the only mechanism through which political accountability can function. Elections are meaningful only if voters can hear criticism of incumbents. Protests are effective only if protesters can denounce government action without fear of prosecution. Journalism serves the public interest only if journalists can investigate and publish their findings without seeking governmental approval. Remove free speech, and elections become rituals, protests become crimes, and journalism becomes public relations. The entire architecture of democratic self-governance depends on the knowledge that no speaker can be silenced, no matter how uncomfortable their message.

V. The Dignity of Counterspeech: Why Suppression Undermines the Vulnerable

Perhaps the most paradoxical consequence of speech suppression is that it ultimately harms the very populations it purports to protect. When a government suppresses "hate speech," it creates the illusion that the problem of hatred has been addressed—when in fact it has merely been driven underground, where it festers unchallenged by public debate, counterspeech, and moral persuasion.

The great champions of racial equality in American history understood this intuitively. Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington, W.E.B. Du Bois, Martin Luther King Jr., and Malcolm X all operated under various forms of speech restriction—both legal and extralegal—and all insisted that their capacity to speak freely was essential to their liberation. King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail" is, among other things, a profound argument about the moral necessity of open discourse: the injustices of segregation were exposed and challenged precisely because speakers were willing to voice truths that offended the powerful. The civil rights movement succeeded not because the state protected its speakers but because it persisted despite the state's hostility—and because the moral force of its arguments, spoken openly, ultimately persuaded a nation.

Counterspeech is not merely an alternative to censorship; it is a superior one, because censorship addresses the symptom while leaving the underlying belief intact, whereas counterspeech engages the idea itself and offers the possibility of genuine persuasion. A society that responds to racism with arrests rather than arguments has not defeated racism; it has merely declared it illegal, leaving the belief system intact and perhaps even strengthening it through the martyrdom effect.

Moreover, hate speech laws disproportionately affect marginalized communities. In the United Kingdom, the NAACP-equivalent organization, the Runnymede Trust, documented that hate speech prosecutions fell disproportionately on ethnic minorities and those expressing anti-establishment views. In Germany, Holocaust denial laws have been used more frequently against obscure individuals than against powerful neo-Nazi figures. In France, the Gayssot Act has been used against those questioning aspects of the official WWII narrative while leaving mainstream Holocaust revisionists untouched. The power to define "hate" always favors the more powerful interpreter, and the history of coded legal suppression—from laws against "anti-social behavior" to "public order" offenses targeting targeted communities—demonstrates that those with less political power are consistently more vulnerable to the enforcement of vaguely defined speech crimes.

The argument for counterspeech is ultimately an argument for human dignity. To tell a subjugated people, "We will silence those who hate you," is to treat them as wards of the state rather than as agents of their own liberation. The only response consistent with the equal dignity of all persons is to empower every person with the tools of persuasion, argument, and moral witness—and to trust that the better argument will prevail when both sides are free to speak.

VI. The Objective Reality of Harm: Government Censorship Causes Greater Harm Than Free Expression

A final consideration demands attention: the measurable, concrete harm caused by government censorship vastly and demonstrably exceeds any harm caused by unregulated speech. When the United States government imposed the Espionage Act during World War I, the result was not a more patriotic or harmonious society but the imprisonment of thousands of dissenters, the destruction of the socialist press, and the suppression of legitimate debate about the war's wisdom and conduct. When the Soviet Union suppressed "anti-Soviet agitation," the result was not social harmony but the entrenchment of a regime that killed millions of its own citizens—and whose crimes could not be spoken of until it was too late. When China criminalized discussion of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests, the result was not the prevention of future unrest but the erasure of historical memory and the perpetuation of authoritarian rule.

These are not tragedies born of too much free expression. They are tragedies born of too little. They are the predictable, inevitable consequences of placing the power to silence in the hands of the state. The direct, physical harms caused by government censorship—imprisonment, ruin of careers, destruction of families, suppression of life-saving information—are concrete and measurable. The alleged harms of unregulated speech—offense, hurt feelings, the propagation of false beliefs—are primarily psychological and are, in any case, not susceptible to cure without recourse to the same state power that has proven so consistently destructive.

The equation is therefore straightforward. Absolute free speech may permit some harms—offense, hurt feelings, the propagation of false beliefs. But the alternative—government-regulated speech—has been demonstrated, repeatedly and across cultures, to produce harms of a categorically different magnitude: the destruction of political liberty, the elimination of dissent, the entrenchment of tyranny, and the suppression of truth itself. The choice is not between a perfect information landscape and a flawed one; it is between a flawed landscape where individuals retain the agency to navigate it and a controlled landscape where the navigator is the state itself.

VII. Objections Addressed

"But what about shouting fire in a crowded theater?"

This famous phrase from Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes's opinion in Schenck v. United States (1919) has been so thoroughly misused as to have become a cautionary tale about the dangers of the very speech restrictions it justified. Schenck was a low moment in First Amendment jurisprudence, and Holmes himself effectively repudiated the reasoning in his dissent in Abrams v. United States months later. In any event, the "crowded theater" analogy proves too much. Creating a genuine, immediate, life-threatening panic is not "speech" in any meaningful sense of expression of ideas; it is directly analogous to any other act of physical sabotage or violence, already criminal under other statutes. It requires no separate speech restriction to address.

"What about targeted harassment and direct threats?"

Targeted, repeated harassment directed at specific individuals and credible threats of violence are, properly understood, not exercises of expression of ideas but direct personal aggression that causes demonstrable, targeted harm to identifiable individuals. They may, like physical assault, be subject to regulation without abridging the freedom of speech in any meaningful sense. The absolute free speech position does not require acquiescence in stalking, doxing with intent to incite violence, or other forms of direct interpersonal aggression. It does, however, insist that the regulation of such conduct be justified on the grounds of direct personal harm—not on the grounds that the expression is offensive, hateful, or untrue.

"Don't other democracies manage with hate speech laws?"

The existence of hate speech laws in other democracies proves only that those countries have accepted a different, more restrictive standard of free expression. It does not demonstrate that those countries are more free, more equal, or more just. In fact, the empirical evidence suggests otherwise. The countries with the strongest protections for hate speech—the United States foremost among them—have vibrant, contentious public spheres in which marginalized voices are free to organize, protest, and persuade. The countries with the most restrictive speech regimes—Russia, China, Turkey, Venezuela—are authoritarian states where speech regulation serves principally to entrench power. The correlation between speech restriction and authoritarian governance is not coincidental; it is causal.

VIII. The Moral Argument: Autonomy and Human Dignity

Beyond considerations of political strategy and historical prudence, an absolute free speech principle rests on a deeper philosophical foundation: the moral autonomy of the human person.

To possess a right of free expression is to possess the dignity of a thinking, speaking agent—a dignity that cannot be maintained if the right to speak is conditional on the approval of the state. Kant's categorical imperative demands that we treat humanity, in ourselves and others, always as an end and never merely as a means. When we empower the state to decide what may and may not be said, we reduce the speaker to a means of achieving the state's preferred social outcome—harmony, offensiveness reduction, informational accuracy. We treat the speaker not as an autonomous agent with the right to reach their own conclusions and express them freely but as an instrument of social policy whose speech may be directed, permitted, or suppressed as the state sees fit.

This degradation is no less real for being abstract. Every instance of state censorship communicates a single, unmistakable message to the speaker: your judgment is not worthy of respect, your voice is not worthy of hearing, your conclusions are too dangerous for public discourse. This is fundamentally incompatible with the conception of equal human dignity that underlies the entire democratic project.

Moreover, the right to hear is as fundamental as the right to speak. When the state suppresses an idea, it denies not only the speaker's right to express it but every citizen's right to encounter, evaluate, and respond to it. A citizenry denied access to the full range of ideas—including ideas that are offensive, false, or dangerous—is not a free citizenry but a managed one. And the history of managed populations is a history not of social peace but of intellectual impoverishment and political subjugation.

Conclusion

An absolute interpretation of free speech is not a radical position. It is, historically and philosophically, the default position of the democratic tradition. It is the position that animated the American founders, who understood from direct experience with British censorship that the power to suppress ideas was the power to suppress liberty itself. It is the position that sustained the abolitionist movement, the women's suffrage movement, the labor movement, the civil rights movement, and the LGBTQ+ rights movement—all of which required the freedom to say things that the powerful found dangerous, offensive, and subversive.

The alternatives—hate speech laws, misinformation regulations, protections from offense—are not moderate compromises between liberty and order. They are the first steps on a well-worn path toward the concentration of power in the hands of those who define acceptable speech. They channel the very tool of authoritarian control through the institutions of democratic governance, dressing censorship in the language of inclusion, safety, and truth. The seduction of this approach lies in its apparent reasonableness: who could possibly oppose the regulation of hate, the suppression of lies, or the protection of the vulnerable? The answer is that these categories dissolve upon contact with the reality of state power, leaving only the capacity to silence.

The absolute position, by contrast, trusts human beings to navigate a world of dangerous ideas—to encounter hate and respond with moral courage, to meet falsehood with truth, to answer offense with the strength of their own convictions rather than the intervention of the state. It is a position of radical, even frightening, optimism about human agency. But it is the only position consistent with the recognition that we are free beings, not subjects; citizens, not wards; speakers, not supplicants.

The price of liberty, it has been said, is eternal vigilance. The price of free speech is the willingness to tolerate that which we find intolerable—and to meet it with nothing more than the force of our own words. That is not merely a legal principle; it is the defining commitment of a free people. Absolute free speech is not the enemy of a just society. It is the only foundation upon which a just society can be built, maintained, and renewed.

The choice, as it has always been, belongs to those who refuse to trade freedom for the false promise of safety.

The Absolutist Free Speech Position: Arguments and Reasoning

Core Philosophical Foundations

The Slippery Slope Argument

The central concern is that once any exception to free speech exists, the principle itself becomes unstable. The reasoning proceeds:

  1. Every restriction requires someone to draw a line
  2. Those drawing the line exercise power, which is subject to bias, political pressure, and error
  3. Today's "reasonable restriction" becomes tomorrow's tool for broader suppression
  4. Powers granted for "good reasons" don't stay confined to those reasons

Historical cases frequently cited include how laws against hate speech in some democracies have been used against minority groups, political dissidents, or journalists rather than just their intended targets.

The Epistemic Humility Argument

Absolutists argue that no authority can reliably distinguish harmful speech from valuable speech:

  • Yesterday's scientific consensus often becomes today's outdated idea
  • Speech widely considered dangerous at one time may later be recognized as legitimate dissent (civil rights arguments, climate warnings, anti-war positions)
  • The "marketplace of ideas" functions better when there's no gatekeeping about which ideas may enter
  • What society calls "misinformation" is frequently contested knowledge in real time

The Dissident Protection Argument

Free speech restrictions are argued to disproportionately harm marginalized voices:

  • Established power structures define what counts as "hate speech" or "misinformation"
  • Social media content moderation has historically enforced dominant cultural narratives
  • Political minorities, protesters, and whistleblowers rely on expansive speech protections
  • Authoritarian regimes consistently begin with some "reasonable" exception (anti-extremism, anti-fake-news) and expand from there

The Marketplace of Ideas Framework

John Milton and John Stuart Mill's legacy

The classical liberal tradition argues:

  • Truth emerges from collision, not protection from falsehood
  • Even false speech serves a purpose by forcing truth to be actively defended and thus better understood
  • A belief held without exposure to challenge becomes "dead dogma" rather than genuine understanding
  • Mill's "harm principle" draws the line at direct incitement to immediate violence but not at offensive or false ideas

Counter-Speech as the Preferred Solution

Rather than restriction, absolutists advocate:

  • Responding to bad arguments with better arguments
  • Building critical thinking capacity rather than relying on censorship
  • Platform-level responsiveness rather than legal prohibition
  • Social consequences (criticism, deplatforming by private actors) being acceptable while state prohibition is not

Specific Arguments About Hate Speech

Definitional Problems

Absolutists highlight that "hate speech" is notoriously difficult to define consistently:

  • Religious texts contain passages others find hateful
  • Political speech about immigration, identity, or statistics about group differences can be characterized as hateful
  • Satire, art, and academic analysis may superficially resemble hate speech
  • Cross-cultural definitions vary enormously
  • Courts applying hate speech laws show significant inconsistency

The Empirical Uncertainty Argument

  • Evidence that hate speech laws actually reduce hatred or discrimination is contested
  • Some comparative research suggests societies with strong speech protections can still have high social cohesion
  • Removing hate speech doesn't address underlying social dynamics driving prejudice
  • The causal link between speech and harm is often assumed rather than rigorously demonstrated

The Counterspeech Point

Hate speech often backfires by drawing attention to the views expressed (the Streisand Effect), and suppression gives persecuted ideas credibility.

Specific Arguments About Misinformation

The Fallibility Problem

  • Every era's "misinformation" has sometimes included views later vindicated
  • Public health messaging during COVID-19 changed repeatedly while being presented as definitive
  • Intelligence community claims about WMDs in Iraq were officially promoted misinformation
  • Climate science, dietary advice, and economic policy have all involved contested claims that institutions pushed as settled truth
  • Who decides? The concern is that state or platform designation of "misinformation" privileges current institutional consensus over legitimate dissent

The Demand-Side Argument

  • The problem isn't primarily supply of false ideas but demand for them driven by psychological, social, and institutional factors
  • Improving media literacy, scientific education, and institutional trustworthens the public's ability to evaluate claims
  • Censoring false claims doesn't address why people believe them

Principled Arguments

Autonomy and Dignity

  • Free expression is tied to individual self-authorship and autonomy
  • Being told you cannot express your views (even wrong ones) treats you as less than a full agent
  • The right to be offensive is part of the right to be an independent thinker

Anti-Paternalism

  • Restrictions assume people are fragile and cannot be trusted with offensive or false ideas
  • This is inherently paternalistic—it removes individuals' capacity to judge for themselves
  • A liberal society should treat citizens as capable of evaluating ideas

Democratic Legitimacy

  • Citizens in a democracy need access to the full range of political ideas to make informed choices
  • Speech restrictions by government inherently corrupt democratic self-governance
  • Even protection for fringe views ensures democratic accountability

The Asymmetry of Power Argument

  • Those with power define "acceptable" discourse
  • Speech regulations inevitably reflect the interests and biases of whoever governs
  • History shows expanded speech restrictions correlate more with authoritarian drift than with reduced social harm

Private vs. Public Distinction

An important nuance: most absolutists distinguish between:

Government prohibition - what the state can punish you for saying Private consequences - what individuals, platforms, or communities can do (ignore, criticize, boycott, ban from private platforms)

This distinction allows absolutists to oppose legal censorship while accepting that individuals and companies exercise their own speech rights by choosing what speech to associate with.

Common Objections That Absolutists Address

"What about shouting fire in a crowded theater?"

  • Holmes's famous example referred to direct, immediate, demonstrable harm—already existing legal categories like incitement, fraud, and true threats don't require a speech exception

"Doesn't some speech cause real harm?"

  • Absolutists accept restrictions on actions (harassment, threats, fraud) while maintaining that speech itself deserves protection. The challenge is where to draw this line without engulfing political speech.

Summary of the Absolutist Position

The absolutist case rests on a cluster of interconnected arguments:

  1. Institutional skepticism: no authority can be trusted with speech-censoring power
  2. Epistemic humility: we're wrong too often to confidently suppress "wrong" ideas
  3. Historical evidence: speech restrictions are reliably expanded and abused
  4. Principled consistency: protecting only popular speech isn't really protecting speech
  5. Empirical uncertainty: the claimed benefits of restriction are insufficiently demonstrated
  6. Positive alternative: counterspeech, education, and resilience are better long-term solutions

The position isn't necessarily that harmful speech is good, but that the cure of censorship is reliably worse than the disease.

The Unbreakable Foundation: Why Free Speech Must Be Absolute

Delivered at the Annual Symposium on Constitutional Liberty

Friends, fellow citizens, defenders of human dignity —

I stand before you today to make the most important argument that can possibly be made in a free society. Not an argument for left or right. Not an argument for one faction against another. But an argument for the very mechanism — the only mechanism — by which every other right, every other freedom, every other hope for a just civilization survives.

The right to speak freely. Absolutely. Completely. Without apology.

I will not stand here and offer you a measured, reasonable, watered-down version of this principle. Because this is not a principle that survives moderation. The moment you carve out an exception, you hand the carver a knife that never gets returned.

I. The Principle

Every single right you hold dear — the right to vote, the right to worship, the right to assemble, the right to refuse an unlawful search, the right to a fair trial — all of it rests on one foundational pillar: the right to say what you think, even when it makes people uncomfortable. Especially when it makes people uncomfortable.

Because what is the alternative? Who decides which speech is comfortable enough to be permitted? Who holds that power? Have you met human beings?

History answers this question with blood. Every regime, every junta, every despotism that has crushed human freedom began not with a rifle, but with a pen. Not by banning guns, but by banning ideas. The tyrant's first instinct is not violence — it is silence. Silence the critics. Silence the dissenters. Silence the people who inconvenience the powerful with the truth.

And here is the terrifying part: they almost always do it with the public's consent. Every authoritarian movement in history has convinced the public that this particular speech, this particular idea, is too dangerous to be free. "It's different this time," they say. "These ideas are too hateful. These words are too violent. These speakers are too extreme."

And when the public hands over that authority — that power to silence — it creates a machine that can never be safely restarted. Because the machinery of censorship, once built, does not sit idle. It serves whoever operates it. And it will not always be operated by you.

II. The Core Argument

Let me be absolutely clear about why speech must be protected without exception in law:

First — because power corrupts the exceptions.

Tell me: when a government is given the authority to suppress "dangerous" speech, who defines dangerous? Today it might be genuine violence and incitement — and reasonable people may debate that boundary. But tomorrow it becomes "misinformation." The day after, "sedition against the policies of the elected government." Soon after, "undermining public trust in institutions." Each definition grows. Each precedent expands. Each exception swallows more than it was meant to consume.

This is not hypothetical. This is the iron law of censorship: it always expands beyond its original justification. A power granted for the most noble, most universally agreed-upon reasons will be used for the most banal and corrupt reasons within a single generation. It is inevitable. It is gravitational.

Second — because history proves that the "reasonable exceptions" are traps.

The Weimar Republic of Germany had laws against hate speech. They did not prevent the rise of fascism — they provided a legal framework that was eventually repurposed by fascists to silence their opponents.

The Soviet Constitution of 1936 — the Stalin Constitution — guaranteed freedom of speech, freedom of the press, and freedom of assembly. Article 125 of that constitution explicitly protected these rights. But those guarantees came with invisible quotation marks, because speech was only free insofar as it conformed to the interests of the working class — as defined, of course, by the state.

Britain, the mother of parliamentary democracy, prosecuted its own citizens for sedition and seditious libel well into the twentieth century — often targeting exactly the sort of dissenters that history would vindicate as heroes.

Every regime that has restricted speech in the name of order, in the name of tolerance, in the name of protecting vulnerable communities, has eventually turned those restrictions against the very people they claimed to protect. Every. Single. One.

Third — because the cure for bad speech is more speech.

This is not a platitude. It is a structural observation about how human societies actually discover truth. Truth does not emerge from curated, government-approved discourse. It emerges from collision. From friction. From the messy, ugly, often offensive clash of ideas competing in the open air.

You cannot refute an idea you never hear. You cannot expose a lie you are prevented from examining. You cannot build immunity to bad arguments if you quarantine them behind walls of prohibition. Every idea that is silenced does not disappear — it goes underground, where it metastasizes, where it becomes a conspiracy, where it festers in the dark without challenge, antidote, or accountability.

Suppression is the fertilizer of extremism. Open debate is its most powerful antidote.

III. Addressing the Objections

Now, I know what some of you are thinking. I know the objections because they are sincere, and I respect the sincerity even as I reject the conclusion.

"But surely speech that directly incites violence is different!"

Perhaps. And there is already robust law addressing genuine incitement — speech that is specifically and imminently directed to producing lawless action with the intent and likelihood that it will. But notice what happens when we broaden that category: "hate speech," "violent speech," "extremist speech." These categories are infinitely elastic. Today's "hate speech" is tomorrow's dissent. The religious minority that speaks its doctrine will be accused of hate. The dissident who criticizes government policy will be accused of extremism. The margin between incitement and offense is where tyranny lives.

"But what about disinformation that puts public health at risk?"

Ask yourself: who decided what constituted disinformation? And how often were they wrong? During recent global events, governments and platforms suppressed legitimate scientific debate — debate that later proved partially or wholly correct — in the name of combating misinformation. They suppressed discussion of vaccine side-effect data, discussion of early treatment protocols, discussion of lab-origin hypotheses that serious scientists entertained. Not all of these were correct — but the very process of sorting truth from falsehood was the process of open debate, and that process was short-circuited by people who believed they already had the answer and that the public could not be trusted with the question.

This is the perpetual temptation: the gatekeeper always believes the gate is necessary. The censor always believes they are uniquely qualified to distinguish truth from error. The silencer always believes that they will only silence the right things. But you and I must judge not the censor's intentions, but the architecture of the power we are granting them. And that architecture is always, always dangerous.

"But speech causes harm! Words can wound! Psychological damage is real!"

I do not deny that words can cause pain. Words are powerful. That is precisely why their regulation is so perilous — because a power that can punish dangerous words can be turned against anyone whose words the powerful find threatening. The solution to painful speech is not a police state. The solution is to develop thick skin, to build cultures of resilience, to answer speech with speech, and to trust that in a free market of ideas, the truth has an inherent advantage — not because people are perfectly rational, but because no government is more rational than the collective intelligence of a liberated public.

IV. The Deeper Case

But I want to take this argument beyond the pragmatic — beyond "censorship doesn't work in practice." I want to make the moral case, because at bottom, this is moral.

Speech is not merely a tool for democracy. It is an extension of thought itself. To control what a person may say is to claim authority over what that person may think aloud, share, debate, and explore. It is to say: Your mind is your own, but your voice belongs to the state.

What kind of liberty is liberty without the right to express dissent? What kind of freedom of religion exists if you may not speak your theological beliefs openly? What kind of freedom of the press exists if the press may say only what is pre-approved? What kind of political liberty exists if you cannot criticize your government without fear of legal consequence?

None. These freedoms become ornaments. Decorations. Hollow words on parchment.

The absolute protection of speech is not a policy preference. It is a recognition of human sovereignty — the acknowledgment that each human being is a thinking, reasoning, meaning-making creature who has the right to participate in the great, unfinished conversation of civilization without asking permission from any authority.

V. The Responsibility That Comes With This Position

And let me be clear — this is not a comfortable position to hold. It requires moral courage. It means defending the speech of people whose views you find repugnant. It means enduring offense. It means accepting that some people will say ugly, stupid, cruel things and that the legal system must remain indifferent to the content of those things.

This is not because ugly speech is good. It is because the only alternative to a society that tolerates ugly speech is a society that is empowered to define what is ugly — and once that power exists, no one is safe.

The test of your commitment to free speech is not whether you defend pleasant speech. Pleasant speech has never needed protection. The test is whether you defend speech that horrifies you. Whether you defend it legally, not merely socially. Whether you recognize that the right to speak free of government punishment is universal — or it is meaningless, because it cannot be selectively denied without being effectively destroyed.

VI. A Warning and a Hope

I will leave you with both.

The warning: We are living in a moment — not unique in history, but certainly dangerous — where the technology of communication has made censorship more powerful than at any point in human history. Where governments and private platforms possess the capacity to surveil, suppress, and silence speech at a scale and with a precision that Orwell could only imagine. Where the temptation to use that power for seemingly good purposes is overwhelming. Where the cultural appetite for safety, for comfort, for protection from offense, is eroding the will to tolerate the wild, chaotic, sometimes offensive reality of free expression.

The machinery of suppression is being built as we speak. Often by people with good intentions. Almost always with the promise that this time, it will be different. This time, the power will be used wisely. This time, it will be wielded only against true evil.

Do not believe it. The machinery does not care who built it. It serves whoever holds the levers. And those levers will not always be in the hands of people you trust.

The hope: The same technology that enables suppression also enables speech to spread further and faster than ever before. Ideas that governments have suppressed for centuries now circulate freely. Dissent that once required printing presses and underground networks now reaches millions in seconds. The human hunger for expression, for debate, for truth — that hunger has not been dulled. It is as old as language itself and as persistent as breath.

The case for free speech is not lost. It has never been fully won, and it never will be — because it must be won again in every generation, in every culture, in the face of every new technology and every new authoritarian temptation.

VII. The Conclusion

So I ask you — no, I implore you —

Do not bargain away this freedom for the sake of feeling safer. Do not trade the right to speak for the promise of being shielded from words that wound. Do not hand the powerful a tool that history proves they will inevitably use against you.

Stand for absolute legal protection of speech. Not because all speech is good. But because no authority can be trusted to decide which speech is good. Not because offense is trivial. But because the power to punish offense is infinitely more dangerous than offense itself.

Defend the right of every person to say what they believe — the wise and the foolish, the kind and the cruel, the right and the wrong. Protect the marketplace of ideas, not because the market is perfect, but because it is the only alternative to a state-controlled monopoly on truth.

And never forget: the right that exists only when the government approves of the message is not a right at all. It is a privilege. And privileges are revoked.

The guarantee of free speech is the guarantee that you — all of you, every one of you — remain the sovereign of your own mind and your own voice.

Defend it absolutely. Or watch it disappear entirely.

Thank you.

The argument here advocates for a position on one end of a genuine and ongoing democratic debate. Engaging seriously with multiple perspectives on this subject is itself an exercise consistent with the values expressed above.

Today, the definition of hate speech may target racial slurs; tomorrow, it could be used to criminalize religious critiques, political satire, or advocacy for unpopular social causes. By protecting even the most vile and reprehensible expression, we establish a robust legal barrier that prevents the government from deciding which identities, beliefs, or viewpoints are worthy of protection. The right to speak freely must include the right to offend, because offense is subjective. What is deeply offensive to one community may be sacred truth or necessary political critique to another. To legislate against offense is to legislate against disagreement itself.

Critics of absolute free speech often argue that unchecked expression causes real-world harm, inciting violence or perpetuating systemic inequality. While the emotional and psychological impact of hateful rhetoric is undeniable, the legal remedy lies not in censorship, but in more speech. The most effective antidote to bad speech is not enforced silence, but persuasive counter-speech. When society relies on the state to suppress harmful ideas, it atrophies its own moral and intellectual muscles, becoming dependent on authority rather than engaging in the difficult work of persuasion and community building. Moreover, driving hateful or extremist views underground through legal prohibition does not eliminate them; it merely prevents them from being exposed to the light of public scrutiny and rebuttal. Openly confronting these ideas allows society to identify, challenge, and isolate them, whereas banning them creates martyrs and fosters resentment.

The preservation of liberty requires a willingness to tolerate the intolerable. The First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, often cited as the gold standard of free speech protection, was designed not to protect popular or polite discourse, but to shield the unpopular, the radical, and the offensive. Once we accept the principle that some speech is too dangerous to be heard, we have accepted the principle that the state knows better than the citizenry what they are allowed to think and say.

Protecting hate speech, misinformation, and offensive content is not an endorsement of their content, but a defense of the process by which free people govern themselves. Here are the core reasons and supposed benefits of adopting such a policy:

1. The Slippery Slope of Censorship

The central argument is that once a government or institution gains the authority to restrict speech based on content, there is no principled limit to what can be censored.

  • Subjectivity of Definitions: Terms like "hate speech" and "misinformation" are inherently subjective and culturally contingent. What one group considers hateful or false, another may view as legitimate criticism or controversial truth.
  • Mission Creep: Historically, powers granted to suppress "dangerous" speech are often expanded to silence political dissent, minority viewpoints, or inconvenient truths. An absolutist policy prevents this creep by removing the mechanism of content-based restriction entirely.

2. The "Marketplace of Ideas"

Proponents argue that truth is best discovered through unrestricted competition among ideas, not through top-down decree.

  • Self-Correction: In an open society, false or harmful ideas are best countered by more speech—facts, logic, and counter-arguments—rather than suppression. Suppression drives harmful ideas underground, where they fester and radicalize without challenge.
  • Resilience of Truth: If an idea is true, it will withstand scrutiny. If it is false, it will be exposed in open debate. Censorship implies a lack of confidence in the public’s ability to discern truth, which undermines democratic agency.

3. Protection of Minority and Unpopular Views

Paradoxically, absolutist free speech is often seen as the strongest protector of marginalized groups.

  • Power Dynamics: Those in power define what is "acceptable." Historically, laws against "seditious" or "offensive" speech have been used disproportionately against civil rights activists, religious minorities, and political dissidents.
  • No Safe Exceptions: If exceptions are made for speech deemed "hateful" by the majority, those same legal tools can be turned against minorities when political winds shift. An absolutist stance ensures that even the most unpopular or offensive minority viewpoints remain protected from state suppression.

4. Prevention of Government Overreach and Arbitrariness

An absolutist policy limits the power of the state and private institutions to act as arbiters of truth and morality.

  • Accountability: Without free speech, citizens cannot fully expose corruption, abuse, or incompetence by those in power. Restrictions on speech, even well-intentioned ones, create blind spots where authority can operate without scrutiny.
  • Avoiding Bias: When platforms or governments decide what constitutes "misinformation," they inevitably inject their own biases. An absolutist approach removes this gatekeeping role, preventing any single entity from controlling the narrative.

5. Individual Autonomy and Dignity

This view holds that adults are capable of making their own judgments about what to believe and say.

  • Paternalism vs. Liberty: Restricting speech to protect people from offense or error is seen as paternalistic. It treats citizens as children who cannot handle difficult or false ideas. Respect for individual autonomy means trusting people to navigate complex information landscapes, even if they sometimes make mistakes.
  • Moral Agency: The freedom to speak, including to offend or err, is integral to human dignity. Suppressing speech denies individuals the right to express their identity, beliefs, and grievances.

6. Social Stability Through Open Pressure Valves

Allowing all speech, including hateful or extreme views, can serve as a societal pressure valve.

  • Visibility Over Suppression: When harmful ideologies are forced into the open, they can be monitored, debated, and socially marginalized through organic community responses rather than state enforcement. Suppression often creates martyrs and fuels conspiracy theories about hidden truths.
  • Reduced Radicalization: Open dialogue allows for the possibility of persuasion and de-radicalization. Censorship can reinforce echo chambers and deepen resentment against perceived oppressors.

Conclusion

From this perspective, the risks of allowing hate speech and misinformation—such as social discord or temporary confusion—are outweighed by the catastrophic risk of empowering authorities to decide what can be said. The absolutist position holds that freedom is indivisible: if you allow exceptions for speech you dislike, you create a precedent that can be used to silence speech you value. Therefore, protecting all speech, no matter how offensive or false, is the only way to ensure that fundamental freedoms remain secure for everyone.
